newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - UK's Howe proud of Hong Kong deal, has fears.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - UK's Howe proud of Hong Kong deal, has fears.

text.p: The man who negotiated the return of Hong Kong to China in 1984 is still proud of his achievement despite the copious criticism dumped on his head ever since.

"I think the deal itself, given that we had almost no cards to play and China could have extinguished Hong Kong's freedom at any time, was remarkable," said former foreign secretary Lord Geoffrey Howe.

When then Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping made clear to former prime minister Margaret Thatcher at an acerbic 1982 meeting that he wanted a deal on the transfer within two years, it was Howe who took charge.
Critics have long asserted that Howe and his team did not do enough to guarantee the colony's freedoms but the former foreign secretary, speaking in an interview, rejected the charges.

Although Deng solved the main problem by devising the "one country, two systems" policy under which the colony was guaranteed a high degree of autonomy for 50 years after the handover, many other problems remained.
Howe said he had to be permanently on his guard to ensure the final 1984 Joint Declaration spelling out the terms of the handover was as specific as possible to avoid future misunderstandings.
He said he always had "the fear that Deng himself might bridle at propositions inserted by others at different stages and assert that 'we can't have too much detail in this'".
DENG'S TWO-SYSTEMS IDEA 'INSPIRED'
It is clear that the soft-spoken Howe was impressed by Deng -- the man who in 1989 gave the order to crush the Tiananmen Square pro-democracy protest -- and his 'one country, two systems' idea.
"(The talks were) made immensely easier by Deng's inspired suggestion. He discussed it with me at some length," said Howe.

"He was a very philosophical man about these things and said this could be the answer to the two Germanies, which were still divided, it could be the answer to the two Koreas, which were and are still divided, and obviously he had it in mind as an answer to China and Taiwan."
For many months the negotiations were shrouded in secrecy and Howe has little time for critics who say he should have kept the people of Hong Kong informed every step of the way.

"I think that's exactly the way in which one had to conduct it, it was a delicate balance all the way, and those who make that sort of comment on secret diplomacy do not understand the business of conducting international relations, nor indeed any other relations," he said testily.
THE HUMAN LIGHTNING CONDUCTOR
After the signing of the Joint Declaration the colony lived quietly until the Tiananmen Square massacre of June 1989 in which hundreds died.
"Tiananmen Square itself, of course, was a shock and had a fearful impact on Hong Kong, China and the outside world," said Howe.

"When I went back to Hong Kong about three weeks after the event I felt like a human lightning conductor. There was an outburst, a vocal demonstration by some spokesman in the course of my speech which demonstrated the strength of feeling."
Howe, now an adviser to a large U.S. law firm, tried to calm nerves by stressing that the Joint Declaration was designed for both good and bad times.

He likened the handover process to running a relay race with a priceless Ming dynasty vase and said governor Chris Patten's decision to introduce democratic reforms without consulting the Chinese first was a tragedy. Beijing cut all links with Patten in protest.
But Howe said it would be wrong to concentrate on the disagreements between the two sides, given how much of his work had remained intact.

"The through train which we constructed in the Joint Declaration has survived in many other respects. The legal system, the chief justice of whom everybody approves, the administrative system... all those things are part of the continuity which the through train was designed to create," he said.
RISK OF MISUNDERSTANDING

Howe, criticised recently for calling on the Hong Kong press to show restraint during the handover, courted further controversy by saying pro-democracy activists should refrain from spreading their beliefs to China.
"Even if only a handful of people have that view of the future, it risks being misunderstood...that's probably my greatest anxiety," he said.
"One country, two systems is a two-way deal. And if Hong Kong is entitled to expect, as she is, freedom from interference or damaging acts from mainland China, then China can expect the same thing."
They key thing to understand was that despite the advances made since 1984, Chinese society still differed vastly from that of the West, he said.

"There is a great risk of misunderstanding. I come back to the Chinese leadership at Tiananmen Square. However wrong we may think it was -- and is -- in the minds of many Chinese leaders the word 'democracy' conjures up destabilising revolution."
Journalists should be careful not to exaggerate the importance of any incident in the near future and portray it either as a serious threat to the stability of Hong Kong or to China itself, he said.
Despite his fears, and the criticism, Howe is sure he was right to negotiate the Joint Declaration.
"I have no doubt whatsoever about my role in all this...it was a huge privilege to be able to play a part in this most extraordinary relationship."
